name: Ohm's law
description: Inside a metal. The rectangle is a conductor seen end-on: its electrons (blue; a few traced with their paths) fly at their thermal speed and bounce off the metal's ions (the dots), a zigzag. Your supply, on the contact at the right end, adds a slow drift along the field to that random motion: a current, in proportion to the voltage, $I = V/R$ (Ohm's law). Make a current between 2.6 and 3.2 flow into the right contact (averaged over $t = 10$ to $40$). At every collision the electrons hand the ions the energy the field gave them: the Joule heat, shown below. A classical model of a metal (its real electrons are a quantum gas): see the physics notes.

reality.represents: Ohm's law inside a conductor (the Drude model)

remarks.detail: The current, the Joule heat and the Hall voltage are not formulas: they come out of the carriers' motion and collisions, σ = nq²τ/m verified against the Boltzmann equation.
At every collision the carriers hand the lattice the energy the field gave them: the heat is the field's work on the current.

remarks.line: A classical metal, a semiconductor by its ratios
remarks.detail: The carriers are classical particles at the lattice's temperature bouncing off fixed ion cores (the Drude model). A real metal's electrons are a degenerate quantum gas whose own ratios (plasma oscillations per collision, screening per free path) the model cannot afford; its carriers have a lightly doped semiconductor's ratios (the Scales section names which), which conducts by the same laws.

The strip is infinitely long along z, its carriers lines of charge moving as one: currents are per unit length, and the noise is larger than a real conductor's, whose carriers move independently along its length.

A contact takes in the carriers that reach it and gives off as many as keep the layer in front of it neutral, at the lattice's temperature: a perfect reservoir. Real contacts have a resistance, and between different materials a barrier.
